title: One connection. Two decisions.
description: Why proving a player’s identity and forwarding it to a backend are separate steps in Relay.
markdown:
An incoming Minecraft connection crosses more than one boundary. The client first reaches Relay. Relay then chooses a backend and connects to it. A setting that makes sense at one boundary can break the other.

This note follows the distinction in [Relay’s login handler](https://github.com/pustka-sh/Relay/blob/8e61739a675435320c8b0fe48393e30181249082/proxy/src/main/java/dev/relay/session/LoginSessionHandler.java) and the [forwarding configuration](https://github.com/pustka-sh/Relay/blob/8e61739a675435320c8b0fe48393e30181249082/proxy/src/main/resources/relay.default.toml). It is an implementation walkthrough, not a release announcement.

# Who is joining?

Authentication answers a question about the player arriving at the proxy. With online authentication enabled, Relay verifies the player through Minecraft’s session service. With offline authentication, that verification does not happen.

The authentication choice belongs at the network entrance. It does not, by itself, tell a Paper backend how to read identity information sent by a proxy.

# What does the backend trust?

Forwarding is the next conversation. A backend needs to receive the player’s identity using the forwarding mode it expects. Relay and the backend must agree on that mode and, for modern forwarding, the shared secret.

Paper behind a proxy has its own authentication settings. Leaving backend `online-mode` enabled while configuring proxy forwarding can produce a setup that looks reasonable in two separate configuration files and fails when the files are used together. The [setup checker](/tools#setup-check) compares those files because the relationship between their values matters.

A forwarding secret protects the forwarding exchange. It does not replace controlling who can reach a backend. The backend should only accept connections from the proxy through the network’s firewall or equivalent private networking rules. See the [current setup guide](/docs/quickstart) for the actual configuration.

# Status is a different path

The server list status request is not a player login. A successful status response can establish that an address answers Minecraft status requests. It does not prove that authentication, backend selection, and forwarding will succeed for a joining player.

That is why a reachable server and a working login are different observations. Check the step where the connection stops rather than treating every failure as a forwarding problem.

# Follow the boundary

The [Relay Lab](/lab/relay) makes these stages visible: handshake, authentication, routing, backend connection, and forwarding. Its scenarios are illustrative traces in the browser. They do not connect to a running proxy or certify a deployment.

Start with one setting change and follow the affected stage. Then compare the explanation with the source revision linked by the Lab. For an actual network, use the setup checker and the proxy and backend logs alongside that model.

title: Words that point back to code.
description: Inside the documentation pipeline: Java comments, checked examples, and a source revision on every page.
markdown:
An API page is useful only if it describes the code someone is building against. Pustka’s documentation packages keep guides, Java declarations, and a source commit together, rather than letting the website quietly combine unrelated revisions.

# One package, one source revision

A project declares its guides in `pustka.docs.json`. The packaging command reads those Markdown files and combines them with a Java API artifact produced by the documentation toolchain. The resulting package records the project, documentation version, source commit, and source ref.

The site checks that identity against its project registry before accepting a signed publication. The signing key stays in the publishing environment. Visitors receive the rendered documentation and revision information, not the key.

These pieces are visible in the [package builder](https://github.com/pustka-sh/Site/blob/8e73d20447b6f2a378336606591726d9b8028b6e/scripts/package-docs.mjs), [publication service](https://github.com/pustka-sh/Site/blob/8e73d20447b6f2a378336606591726d9b8028b6e/server/services/documentation.mjs), and [Relay’s documentation workflow](https://github.com/pustka-sh/Relay/blob/8e61739a675435320c8b0fe48393e30181249082/.github/workflows/docs.yml). These links capture the implementation this note describes.

# Ask the compiler about Java

The Java doclet works with the compiler’s view of the project. It extracts declarations, parameters, return types, source positions, and authored documentation comments. That gives the website useful structure without treating a text search through `.java` files as a Java parser.

There is still a human boundary: a declaration does not explain itself. When a comment is missing, the reader says so. A public Java method is also not automatically a supported integration API; compatibility policy needs to be stated by the project.

# Make examples earn their place

Relay’s documentation checks compile the Java examples against the project and compare their contents with the Markdown fences that readers copy. A change to one side without the other fails the check.

Compilation establishes that an example uses real declarations with compatible types. It does not establish that a network exchange succeeds, that a callback runs on a particular thread, or that every failure case has been handled. Those behaviors still need their own tests and clear explanations.

# Preserve what a version means

Development documentation follows `main` and can advance with a newer signed publication. Published release documentation is preserved: the same release version cannot be replaced with a different package.

Each page links to its exact source commit, so a reader can inspect the implementation even after development moves on. When comparing versions, structural changes are useful review cues; they do not provide a complete binary or runtime compatibility verdict.

The result is a small, explicit contract: the page can tell you which code it describes, which words came from that code, and which checks its examples passed. Start from the [documentation directory](/docs/projects) to inspect the packages that have actually been published.
